ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Footage from the emergency services ministry shows crews dragging hoses through debris as thick smoke rises over the site in Kolpino. No injuries were reported and officials did not say what caused the fire. The blaze came as Ukraine said it was widening a drone campaign against Russian logistics hubs. Kyiv's defence ministry announced on Saturday it was turning its attention to Ozon, Russia's second-largest online marketplace, after weeks of strikes on rival Wildberries. Two other Ozon warehouses were hit over the weekend, in the Samara and Orenburg regions. Ozon said operations at the Orenburg hub were suspended. https://www.dw.com/en/us-sanctions-halt-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5KUHP Until recently, some educational activities in Iran were exempt from US sanctions Image: Pond5 Images/imago images Advertisement Iranian students hoping to study abroad are facing a new obstacle after TOEFL and GRE testing was suspended inside the country following changes to US sanctions regulations . "My entire plan was built around taking this exam," a TOEFL candidate in Tehran told DW. She said she had spent months preparing applications for a PhD program, contacting professors and gathering documents despite internet disruptions and other challenges. ETS, the US-based organization that administers both exams, announced it suspended testing in Iran after the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) froze General License G, which had allowed certain educational services to continue in Iran . "Following OFAC's suspension of General License G, ETS has paused administration of the TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran effective immediately," the organization said in an official notice. ETS added that Iranian nationals can still take the exams outside Iran and that it is exploring options to restore testing. TOEFL is a US-based English-language proficiency test accepted by universities worldwide. The GRE, also administered by the same US organization, is a standardized test required by some graduate programs, particularly in the United States and Canada. Since the Iran war began in late February, the US has increasingly expanded sanctions targeting Iranian trade and exports, contributing to broader disruptions throughout the Iranian economy . No timeline for testing to resume An Iranian institution that administered TOEFL exams told DW that new registrations had stopped following the latest sanctions changes . The institution added that the suspension could be temporary, but no date had been given for exams to resume. That uncertainty is particularly serious for students approaching university and scholarship deadlines who have spent months preparing documents, contacting professors and paying application-related costs. The suspension follows earlier problems with IELTS (British equivalent of TOEFL) testing in Iran. An IELTS center in Tehran told DW that sanctions-related difficulties transferring money had become one of the main obstacles to continuing exams. Some Iranian applicants had already been traveling to countries such as Turkey and Armenia to take IELTS. TOEFL and GRE candidates may now have to do the same. Can Iran survive Trump's new sanctions? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Rising costs for applicants Alireza, who is preparing to apply to a university in Italy, said the suspension of TOEFL had disrupted a backup plan he had arranged after IELTS testing became unavailable. "European universities usually accept IELTS. But because IELTS has been suspended in Iran, after extensive correspondence with the university, they agreed to let [Iranian students] meet the required score through an equivalent TOEFL result," he told DW. "But now TOEFL has also been suspended in Iran. Travelling to a neighboring country just to take the exam is very expensive, especially given Iran's current economic situation," added Alireza. Another candidate told DW that taking the exam in Turkey or Armenia would mean paying for travel and at least one night's accommodation on top of the test fee. For students hoping to secure scholarships or full funding, those additional expenses can be significant. Many Iranian students pursue post-graduate education abroad Image: Sigrid Gombert/Image Source/IMAGO Students launch petition Iranian TOEFL and GRE candidates have launched an online petition urging ETS to restore access to the exams. The petition says thousands of students are losing access to tests required for university admissions, scholarships, graduate programs and other academic opportunities. Many, it says, have spent months preparing, paid exam-related costs and built their application schedules around specific test dates. "Students should not lose years of preparation or their chance to pursue higher education because access to required examinations has suddenly been removed," the petition states. Narges, an Iranian applicant affected by the suspension, said she had seen the petition circulating in Telegram groups used by language learners and students applying to foreign universities. "I doubt it will have any impact," she said. "Still, I'm going to sign the petition." Experiences of international PhD students navigating Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The organizers are calling on OFAC to provide a specific exemption for standardized academic testing and on ETS to restore TOEFL and GRE services in Iran as soon as legally possible. They argue that sanctions aimed at the Iranian government should not restrict educational opportunities for ordinary citizens who have no role in state policy. When sanctions impact education Until recently, the General License G had provided a legal channel for certain academic exchanges and educational services despite broader US sanctions on Iran . For many students, the suspension is the latest in a series of barriers to studying abroad. Bahar, who is applying for PhD programs, said many Iranian students had already shifted their focus from the United States because obtaining visas had become increasingly difficult. "American universities were our first choice because they generally offer funding for PhD programs more readily than European universities," she told DW. Now, she said, applicants are increasingly turning to Europe and Australia, but the testing suspension has created a new hurdle. Missing a required exam can add months, or even a year, of waiting for affected applicants Image: Rainer Unkel/Imago Images "There is effectively no difference between IELTS and TOEFL for us now, because in either case, we have to leave Iran to take an English language test," Bahar said. For students approaching admissions deadlines, postponement may not simply mean waiting a few months. It can mean missing an entire admissions cycle, losing scholarship opportunities or delaying academic plans by a year or more. While ETS says it is examining possible ways to restore testing in Iran, there is currently no indication of when that might happen. For many applicants, the immediate choice is limited: wait without knowing when testing will return, or spend considerably more to take the same exam abroad. https://www.dw.com/en/beijing-faces-its-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PQfz Prefer DW on Google Although no government has officially confirmed the meeting, some media outlets have already dubbed it 'the new Yalta' Image: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China , Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen next week. China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place. However, a Chinese Foreign Ministry official recently told the press that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. In Moscow, a Kremlin representative said work on "coordination" was underway. The clearest indication about the potential summit came from US President Donald Trump last weekend. Talking to reporters at a Florida airport, Trump said he "thinks" one of the meetings planned for APEC will be with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping . Trump, Putin or Xi: Who really runs the world? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Is the world set for a 'new Yalta'? Despite the lack of official confirmation from either Beijing, Moscow, or Washington, the media has already dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta," invoking the optics of the US, UK, and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II and deciding on the new geopolitical power balance in the Crimean resort town. The Yalta summit saw Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill represent the three main victorious powers of WWII Image: RIA Novosti/SNA/imago At the same time, nobody seems to be quite sure what the three leaders would talk about if China agrees to host the trilateral summit at APEC. In his brief remarks to reporters on Sunday, Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine when asked about the possibility of the meeting, bringing up only "Iran" and "denuclearization" as possible talking points. The Chinese Foreign Ministry reported "no information" when questioned earlier this week about the potential substance of talks. End of campaign to isolate Putin? A three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Russia's President Putin. Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin chief has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies , most notably the US under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden. Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump . The Wall Street Journal has reported that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine. For the US, the president standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a bad look, although Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term. As host, China is in an even trickier position. While Russia and China are broadly aligned on many issues , Beijing does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm China's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability . EU wary of being left out of Ukraine talks The Chinese government is also working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. The European powers would likely bristle at a summit hosted by China and discussing the war in Ukraine without Kyiv or Brussels present at the table. Europe seeks role in Ukraine peace talks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "China is clearly uneasy about the possible trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, and although Beijing has shifted its position from saying nothing to admitting that the three powers are in contact, the vagueness of these declarations seems deliberate," Alicja Bachulska, Asia policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW. "Beijing is aware of the potential negative optics of the 'Yalta 2.0' framing, even if this historical comparison is inaccurate and does not reflect current geopolitical dynamics," Bachulska said. She notes the trilateral meeting could "trigger further escalation in the already worsening relations between China and the EU" if Ukraine is discussed with no Europeans in the room. For China, there is also little to gain in terms of optics. Images of Xi standing with Trump, the leader of Beijing's top rival, and Putin, Beijing's partner in opposing the US, could present an awkward look. "Even if the meeting only yields a photo opportunity, it could nevertheless severely erode China's image," Bachulska added. Beijing and Moscow stick to 'no limits' partnership Putin and Xi have met some 40 times since the Chinese president came to power in 2012. The two neighboring countries have grown especially close following the declaration of "no limits" partnership accord in early 2022. The move was announced by Xi and Putin on the sidelines of Beijing Winter Olympics, just weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The current Russia-China ties are deeper than they have been in decades. At the core of the axis between the two nations is a long-term strategy to contain US power while fostering an alternative global order both Moscow and Beijing can use for their own ends. China helping Russia from the sidelines Throughout the course of the Ukraine war, which is nearing the end of its fifth year with no solution in sight, Beijing has quietly provided Russia with crucial market for energy exports, while supplying technology and so-called "dual-use" goods. While China did not explicitly provide Russia with weapons, its exports included high-tech components that could be used for modern weapons systems like drones. Russia needs China trade more than ever To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Officially, Beijing maintains neutrality on the Ukraine war and has refused to take responsibility for its outcome . "China is more interested in reforming global governance in ways that reflect its preferences and red lines while preserving a collegial appearance," Aurelio Insisa, senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW. Even if China agrees to host the meeting, it will likely avoid framing it as three top powers making decisions for the rest of the world, according to Insisa. "Embracing the 'G3' narrative would undermine its image as a champion of the Global South and developing countries. It is also worth noting that Beijing has shown no interest in engaging with the one pressing issue that could realistically be addressed in such a trilateral format: nuclear disarmament," he added. What are the actual limits of China-Russia axis? In a report published in August, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), painted China as a "decisive enabler" of Russia's war in Ukraine. Beijing was "converting Moscow's dependence into lasting military, technological, economic, and geopolitical advantages while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance," according to the US body. However, the commission also noted there were limits to Beijing's strategic support, and intelligence and security concerns remain a constraint on deeper cooperation. The report emphasizes the relationship is more of a strategic alignment than an alliance, with deep mistrust remaining in some key areas. Russian defense firms, for instance, have accused Chinese companies of stealing intellectual property. Beijing, on the other hand, is concerned with Russia's growing strategic relationship with North Korea , which has reduced Pyongyang's dependence on China. Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video China and Russia also differ on nuclear doctrine. While Beijing maintains a longstanding "no first use" policy, Moscow uses nuclear threats as part of its strategy. China getting a 'privileged vantage point' on Ukraine war But for now, the benefits of alignment remain. MERICS' analyst Insisa believes the cooperation between Russia and China will largely continue within this year's framework, including Russia providing energy and potentially transfering military technology in the "few remaining areas where it retains an advantage." "China, in turn, will continue to supply dual-use technologies, purchase Russian energy, provide Moscow with a measure of diplomatic cover, and — more importantly — offer channels for circumventing Western sanctions," he added. Notably, China will also get a "privileged vantage point" on how the battlefield in Ukraine is evolving land warfare. "Strategic distrust between the two sides, particularly Russia's concerns about economic dependence on China, will continue to limit the scope of their cooperation," Insisa said.
